newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK SFO not to probe NatWest Markets loss.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK SFO not to probe NatWest Markets loss.

text.p: Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO) said on Wednesday it will not launch a criminal investigation into losses incurred by NatWest Markets in interest rate options, a decision likely to rekindle the debate on Britain's fraud laws

The SFO, which investigates cases of serious or complex fraud, said that in the NatWest case the public interest would best be served by the matter being dealt with by markets regulator the Securities and Futures Authority which has the power to fine individuals and bar them from working in the financial markets.

"The SFO has carefully considered the circumstances surrounding the losses incurred by NWM in the interest rate options business and has decided that an investigation with a view to a criminal prosecution is not justified," the SFO statement said.
Earlier this year, the investment banking arm of National Westminster Bank Plc revealed a loss of 90 million pounds ($151 million) in the interest rate options market.
The losses led to the resignation of its chief executive Martin Owen and other senior staff.
The SFO said its director Rosalind Wright had taken into account the nature of the transactions involved, which were highly complex, and the powers of the regulatory authorities in this area.
"She takes the view that the public interest in... this case would be more appropriately satisfied by the matter being dealt with by regulation," the statement added.

The SFA, which regulates market trading, said it was continuing to study a report into the affair produced for NatWest by law firm Linklaters & Paines and accountants Coopers & Lybrand and is reviewing the role of a number of individuals.
An SFA spokesman said the regulator would "undoubtedly have to gather additional information" and could not predict when this process would be completed.
NatWest Markets said it accepted the SFO's decision and noted that it had co-operated fully.
The report showed that the losses were deliberately hidden for over two years by the creation of false profits and unauthorised transfers between trading books at the bank.
The initial losses, in mark and sterling interest rate options, were due to poor trading made worse by adverse market conditions but it said no personal gain was made and no client lost out.
This was probably a crucial factor in the SFO's deliberations, but if false accounting went on to hide the loss then many will feel that a criminal prosecution was in order.
But legal sources said the main difference between the NatWest Markets case and others routinely handled by the SFA was only one of scale.
The fact that the interest rate options market is and esoteric and highly complex one also meant that the facts of the case would have been very difficult to explain to a jury.
Wright, who has only been in her job since April, has already raised the possibility that fraud trials could be tried by an expert panel presided over by a judge rather than by a lay jury.
Ironically, this would be similar to the system used by the SFA, which Wright left to join the SFO, in its disciplinary tribunals.
Wright has also said she is in favour of a single "fraud" offence to simplify trials and the SFO has already made representations on the subject to Britain's Law Commission.
